newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu strains relations with friendly Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu strains relations with friendly Jordan.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hardline policies have strained relations even with Jordan, the only Arab neighbour that did not express alarm at the election of the new Israeli leader.

Although Israeli officials tried on Wednesday to play down a stream of criticism from King Hussein and those around him, the public attacks were unprecedented from an Arab leader who had enthusiastically cultivated ties ever since he made peace with the Jewish state in 1994.
"Israeli officials believe the sharp deterioration in the tight relations with Jordan is the most worrying aspect of Israel's relations with the Arab world," Israeli army radio said.
"The peace with Jordan is in a state of crisis -- not just more tension, but a collapse of the entire fabric of trust, dialogue and discrete contacts between the two states."

King Hussein, who had secret dealings with Israel for years before the treaty, ignored widespread antipathy among Jordanians to the peace agreement even after the election last May of an Israeli government that rejected the land-for-peace basis of Middle East peace talks.
But Netanyahu's actions have left King Hussein exposed in two key areas at a time when Jordanians are still waiting for the promised economic benefits of peace.
Israel's decision to open a new entrance to a controversial tunnel near a revered mosque appeared to infringe the king's traditional role as protector of Moslem holy sites in Jerusalem.

Netanyahu's uncompromising stance toward Palestinians -- ruling out independence, any control in Arab East Jerusalem and reluctance to even talk -- angered Jordanians of Palestinian refugee origin, generally considered a majority of the kingdom's population.

"We understand that the Jordanian government cannot appear to be in opposition to the Arab position," David Bar-Illan, an aide to Netanyahu told Reuters, denying there was any real problem with Jordan.

"We are not alarmed at all," he said, dismissing concern over the tunnel or that Israel's relations with Palestinians had an impact on Jordan. "We feel relations on all levels are continuing at the same level of friendship." .

But comments this week from Jordan -- including the king, the crown prince and a speech in the United States by his wife Queen Noor -- pointed to deep concern that the Arab-Israeli conflict has not been consigned to history by the peace process launched by Washington five years ago.

"Does Israel want to return to the fortress mentality and an arrogant feeling of power?" King Hussein asked in an interview with the Saudi-owned Arabic newspaper Asharq al-Awsat. "I've had the chance to know the Israelis quite well and I'm worried about them."
Jordanian officials had explained their charge to make peace with Israel's previous Labour government in 1994 as partly driven by the belief that a general Arab-Israeli settlement was imminent.
Instead, Israeli talks with Palestinians, Syrians and Lebanese moved slowly even before the election of Netanyahu brought the entire process to a halt.
"The crisis is not only between Israel and Jordan but also between Israel and all the Arab parties," Jordan's ambassador to Israel, Omar al-Rifai, said in an Israel radio interview on Wednesday.
Netanyahu's refusal to consider returning the occupied Golan Heights to Syria has removed the main incentive for Damascus to make peace. Lebanon will not move without Syria.

And the Palestinian talks were effectively frozen until an eruption of violence in the last month, which killed 59 Arabs and 15 Israelis, led to the resumption of talks on Israel implementing a previous agreement.

"Until recently, we in Jordan had been firmly convinced that the historic peace process in the Middle East was irreversible," Queen Noor said in a speech at Harvard University on Tuesday. Recent events have "shaken" that belief, she said.
